Why do we need Docker? Before we type a single command, let's follow one web application through its life, and see the problem Docker solves.
The story begins. You're building a web application. It has three parts: a frontend that users see, a backend with the logic, and a database that keeps the data.
For the frontend, you use React and JavaScript. So you install Node J S, N P M, and React.
For the backend, you use Python and Fast A P I. So you install Python three point thirteen, and Fast A P I.
For the database, you use Postgres. You install Postgres eighteen, and set up its config file.
Then you start coding. App dot J S X for the frontend, and main dot pie for the backend.
And it runs! On your PC, every tool and every version fits together.
But here's a question. Does your code stay on your machine forever?
No! Sooner or later, it has to run somewhere else.
Case one. A new teammate joins, to help you build more features. They get a fresh laptop. First, they need your code.
So you share the code, and they try to run it.
Errors! Command not found. No module named uvicorn. Without the same tools and dependencies, the app just can't run.
So every new teammate spends a whole day, just installing things. One day, then another, then another.
Case two. Your users can't use your laptop. So eventually, you deploy the app on a server.
And you set up the server by hand. The same tools, the same versions, the same config. Again.
Finally, it works. Users can use it.
So, installing by hand is too slow. Every new teammate needs a day of installing, and every server needs the same setup, again.
Doing it all manually just doesn't scale.
We need a way to install everything fast, on any machine.
Here's the solution. Pack each part into a box, with everything it needs inside. That box is called an image.
Any machine with Docker can run these boxes. There's nothing else to install. Minutes, not days.
Same boxes, same result, everywhere. A new teammate, or a server: get the boxes, run them, done.

And that's Docker. Docker builds the box, called an image. It ships it anywhere, to a teammate or a server. And it runs it in seconds. A running box is called a container. That's exactly what this course teaches. Let's start with lesson zero, and install Docker!
